title: Render loop dies when world size changes while zoomed out
description: Seen in browser snapshots (4bl.1): after growing the world while zoomed out, fps/draws froze permanently (identical snapshots, drawCalls 0, 74880 instances at zoom 150). Cause: scene.setMaxZoom exists but HexCanvas never calls it when worldRadius changes, so the zoom limit stays at the opening world value (large = 570). On a bigger world the view can then need a window larger than grid capacity; hexGrid.setWindow throws RangeError inside onBeforeRenderObservable, and Babylon _renderLoop only re-queues a frame after _processFrame returns, so one throw stops rendering forever. Fix: call setMaxZoom(maxZoomFor(layout, radius)) in the world watch before the window rebuilds; consider making useHexWindow clamp rather than throw so an overflow cannot kill the loop.
acceptance_criteria: Switching small->large->huge at max zoom keeps rendering; zoom is clamped to the new world limit; a test covers world change pulling zoom in; no RangeError reachable from the render loop.
notes:
Probe numbers (capacity 76800): huge maxZoom should be 95 but stays 570 from large. At 16:9, zoom 127.67 needs 56576, zoom 150.06 needs exactly 76800 (the frozen snapshot had 74880, one step from overflow). Second gap: capacityFor sizes for aspect WIDEST=3, but aspect 3.5 at the correct huge maxZoom 95 needs 95744 > capacity, so a wider-than-3:1 window overflows even after setMaxZoom is wired. Clamp aspect in viewRect or clamp tiles in useHexWindow.
Fix in place, awaiting browser check: HexCanvas pushEverything calls setMaxZoom(maxZoomFor) first (runs on scene create + every world change, before field watcher rebuilds window). Grid capacity = gridCapacity(layout) = max(ZOOM_BUDGET, capacityFor(MIN_MAX_ZOOM)) = 80000, covers any radius not just named sizes. useHexWindow check goes through viewSpan, which clamps aspect to WIDEST=3 so ultrawide cannot overflow. Tests: gridCapacity over radii 10-400, stale large limit on huge overflows (documents the bug), viewSpan at aspect 3.5 fits, camera setMaxZoom clamps immediately. 385 tests, typecheck, lint pass. Verify: huge world <-> large world at max zoom, render keeps going.
close_reason: Verified in browser: large<->huge switches at max zoom, zoom clamps to 95 on huge, render never stalls (85 snapshots, draws always >0)

title: Flat LOD prism renders without instance colours
description: User report after 4bl.3: map turns white-ish past a certain zoom out. Suspected: flat prism material defines computed while its thinInstanceCount is 0 (hidden at creation), so INSTANCESCOLOR is never set; switching to it later does not mark attributes dirty, so it draws with plain diffuse.
acceptance_criteria: Colours identical on both prisms at every zoom; regression test checks the flat prism material defines include instance colour after a switch.
notes: Root cause confirmed by failing test: render loop warming check scene.isReady(false) (4bl.2) evaluates the hidden, empty flat prism, settling StandardMaterial defines with INSTANCESCOLOR=false; later instancing flips INSTANCES but attribute defines are not re-evaluated, so hexes draw plain white diffuse. Fix: grid.setDetail marks material AttributesDirtyFlag after each switch. Regression test in picking.test.ts covers both directions. 431 tests pass. Awaiting browser check.

title: Incremental window moves: only write chunks entering view
description: useHexWindow rebuilds the whole span on each chunk crossing: tilesInSpan allocates a HexTile object per hex (20-80k), grid.setWindow recomputes every matrix and colour, clears/rebuilds indexByKey, and thinInstanceRefreshBoundingInfo walks every instance. A one-chunk pan only changes one row/column of chunks. Diff old vs new ChunkSpan, free slots of leaving chunks, fill entering chunks into freed slots (swap-remove to keep count dense), and set the bounding box analytically from the span instead of refreshing from matrices.
acceptance_criteria: Bench shows single-chunk pan cost proportional to entering chunks, not window size; fog/tint still follow hexes across slot reuse; picking works everywhere in new window (existing hexWindow/hexGrid tests pass plus a test for slot reuse).
notes:
2026-09-13 browser run: large world zooming 205->570 with all 68k hexes loaded shows frameMs 40-72 and fps 11-20 during zoom/pan, while idle at 570 hits 100 fps (0.12 ms). The hitches come from rebuilding the window as zoom changes the chunk span every few frames, not from GPU load. Strong case for incremental window updates.
Implemented with 4bl.6: grid.moveWindow(keep, entering) swap-removes leaving hexes and appends entering ones; useHexWindow uses tilesEntering(from,to) when a previous span exists; bounds kept by hand (reConstruct from translations) instead of thinInstanceRefreshBoundingInfo per move; color upload is partial (count only). bench:window after: large r150 z570 one-chunk pan 49.3 -> 3.3 ms, one-chunk zoom 3.4 ms, full setWindow 30.2 -> 13.6 ms; huge z95 pan 23.6 -> 0.8 ms. 407 tests pass. Awaiting browser check. Remaining O(window) per crossing: HexCanvas fog map rebuild (9tn.20).

Camera max zoom is clamped so the window never exceeds roughly 6,000 instances; seeing the whole world at once is the minimap's job.

title: Waiting banks movement, so one press crosses a whole route
description: A turn spent waiting added the entity's pace to its carried budget, and nothing capped it. A party that stood still for five turns therefore crossed five hexes on the press that finally moved it, which reads as the forward button walking the whole planned path instead of one turn of it. Only a turn spent travelling should earn its pace, and the carry needs a ceiling for an entity whose next step it cannot yet afford.
acceptance_criteria: Waiting for any number of turns leaves the carry where it was; pressing forward after a long wait crosses the pace, not the backlog; a climb still takes two turns of budget for a pace-one party.

title: Store on entities, a queue and a record
description: hexMap store drops travelers, elapsedHours, logAfter, recall, standing, walkedLeg, stepsFor, originStep, arrive, canArrive and finished. It holds entities, turn, a queue of actions, a record of ActionRecords and a snapshot of EntityStates per turn. advanceTurn resolves and appends, rewindTurn reads the snapshot back, skipPhase resolves each turn up to nextPhaseTurn. Acting after a rewind truncates the recorded future. Explored ground is derived from the record rather than accumulated, so rewind scrubs the fog.
acceptance_criteria: Queue, advance, rewind and truncation are unit tested; explored is derived and shrinks on rewind; sight radius is cut to 30% (floor 1) on night turns.

title: Entity and Action types with resolveTurn

Budget adds pacePerTurn then spends while it covers stepCostTurns, which reads off stepCostKm so there is one cost table.
acceptance_criteria: resolveTurn is pure and tested: pace 1 crosses a flat hex a turn, a climb costs two turns of budget, pace 0.5 takes two turns per flat hex with the carry surviving, a new move replaces a standing one mid-route, camp clears carry, an entity with nothing queued still produces a wait row.

title: [epic] Entities and the turn queue
description: Time becomes the master of the map. Hours are replaced by turns (4 to a phase, 8 to a day), travelers become entities with stats (pace, sight, owner, hidden), and nothing moves except by a turn passing: each entity puts an action on a queue, advancing the turn loops the queue and executes every action, and what happened is written as a record keyed by that turn. Rewinding reads the world back out of that record, fog included. Plan: C:\Users\angelo\.claude\plans\recursive-exploring-sketch.md
design: Two halves kept apart: the queue (intent for the next turn, mutable) and the record (what every spent turn actually did, append-only and keyed by turn). A move order stands until spent or replaced, so crossing four hexes is one order, not four. Per-entity turn budget: flat hex 1, climb 2, pace added each turn and the remainder carried. Night shrinks sight to 30% (floor 1) and leaves pace alone. Acting after a rewind truncates the recorded future.

title: Clock: track the hour and draw the day-night dial
description: A twelve-hour phase of day followed by twelve of night, tracked as whole hours elapsed since the crawl began, from which the phase, the hour within it and the day number are derived. Travel spends time: a leg costs its distance at ten kilometres an hour, so one flat hex is an hour and a climb is two, which falls out of the existing step costs. Drawn as a half dome across the top centre of the display over a dark translucent sky, quartered into four watches of three hours by three slashes. A single sun-and-moon emblem rides the arc, stopping at the head of each watch and tilted so its foot points at the centre of the dome, so it steps three times to cross the sky before the phase turns over and it restarts at the near horizon. Stars come out at night. The day and phase read from inside the dome as one capitalized line. Persisted with the rest of the map state.
design: One monotonic hour counter rather than separate phase and hour fields: a single number cannot get out of step with itself, and phase, hour and day are all cheap to derive from it. Ten km an hour is a game abstraction chosen so a flat hex is exactly one hour and a climb exactly two, matching stepCostKm without a second cost table.
acceptance_criteria: Elapsed hours, phase, hour within the phase and day number are derived in the store from one counter; committing a leg advances the clock by its distance at ten km an hour; the dial sits top centre, quartered by three slashes, with the emblem stepping between four positions and tilting to the arc; day and night are distinguishable; the clock survives a reload; unit tested.
notes: Delivered design differs from the original brief in two ways the user asked for during the work: twelve hour dots became a single emblem stepping between four watch positions, and the day/night gradient skies became one dark translucent dome. The emblem is a single combined sun-and-moon image (src/assets/sun-and-moon.png) rather than two sprites, so the phase is told apart by the stars and the capitalized label rather than by the icon.
close_reason: Delivered: hour clock, dome dial, sun-and-moon emblem, persistence. The hour counter underneath it is superseded by the turn clock in hexcrawl_web-t3p.1; the dial itself carries over.

title: Elevation-aware route tracing
description: Hexes are 10km across. A player picks a start and an end hex; the app traces the fastest route across the terrain. Moving to a hex at the same or lower elevation costs 10km; climbing to a higher one costs double, so routes should prefer contouring around hills over climbing them.

title: Zoom-out limit slider, about 50% further on the huge map
description:
User request 2026-10-13: the huge map (WORLD_SIZES.huge = 300) cannot be zoomed out far enough. Full uncapping is deferred for now. Instead, add a slider that sets how far out the camera may zoom (the max zoom threshold).

- The slider's top end depends on the map size. Small and large maps keep roughly today's limits.
- On the huge map the top end should be about 50% further out than today's limit. Today that limit is maxZoomFor() in src/composables/useHexWindow.ts, which is capped by FARTHEST_ZOOM = 200 and by ZOOM_BUDGET.
- The slider's value goes to hexScene.setMaxZoom(). HexCanvas already calls it with maxZoom().
- The slider is a view setting. It is not saved with the map; per-viewer localStorage is fine.

Watch the grid buffers. gridCapacity() sizes the instance buffers from ZOOM_BUDGET, and 50% more zoom on huge needs about 2.25x the hexes in view. An overflow throws inside the render loop and freezes rendering for good (see bd memory on Babylon render-loop gotchas, and viewSpan squeezing to grid.capacity). So either raise the capacity and budget for the huge map, or make sure viewSpan still clamps. Measure the frame rate at the new widest view.

Deferred follow-up: fully uncap zoom-out on the huge map, probably with a cheaper far-zoom representation such as chunk impostors or the minimap texture.
acceptance_criteria: A slider sets the max zoom-out. Its top end scales with map size, and on the huge map it reaches about 1.5x today's limit. No buffer overflow or render freeze at the widest view on any map size. Existing camera and window tests pass, with new tests for the per-size limits.

Full rate when: grid/arrows/tokens/vision/stops mutators called (wrapped in scene.ts), daylight/field/maxZoom/resize, camera target moved (pan/moveTo), iso.settling, tokens.hopping, or materials still compiling (scene.isReady(false) after each frame). title: Drag the minimap view box to pan the main camera
description: MiniMap.vue only handles click (focusOn, smoothed slide). Grabbing the white view rectangle and dragging it should move the overworld camera in lockstep, like dragging a scrollbar thumb. Use pointer capture so leaving the canvas mid-drag keeps tracking. Needs an immediate, clamped camera setter on IsoCamera (focusOn is smoothed and would lag the pointer); a drag must also cancel any focus slide in progress. A plain click with no movement keeps todays focusOn behaviour. Cursor: grab over box, grabbing while dragging.
acceptance_criteria: Dragging the box moves the main view 1:1 with no lag or jump at grab; release leaves camera where dropped; click-without-drag still recenters; target stays inside pan bounds; drag works when pointer leaves the minimap; unit test for minimap pixel <-> world mapping and the new camera setter.
notes: Implemented: IsoCamera.moveTo(x,z) immediate, clamped to pan bounds, cancels focus slide. engine/minimap.ts pure mapping (worldToMinimap, minimapToWorld, viewBox, boxContains) with tests; MiniMap.vue uses pointer events + setPointerCapture: press inside box keeps grab offset, press outside jumps box under pointer once drag passes 3 px, press+release without drag keeps focusOn click. Cursor grab/grabbing/crosshair. Gates green: 395 tests, vue-tsc, eslint, prettier. Pending: browser check.

title: Max zoom follows the world size
description: The camera's zoom-out limit is a constant, so a small world cannot be seen whole and a huge one is barely dented by pulling back. It should follow the world radius: bigger world, further out. The ceiling is the grid, whose buffers are allocated once, so the zoom for any size is capped by a hex budget and the allocation is sized for the largest world the picker offers.
acceptance_criteria: Pulling back on the small world reaches its rim; the huge world allows a far wider view; the grid never has to hold more than the budget, and switching size reclamps the current zoom rather than leaving the view wider than the new limit.
close_reason: maxZoomFor(layout, radius) in useHexWindow: a world zooms out until it fits on screen or the grid budget (80k hexes, floored at 20k) is spent, with a floor of 40. Small 225, large 570, huge 95. camera.setMaxZoom reclamps the live view; the grid is allocated once for the costliest of the offered sizes.

title: Minimap drew the world upside down
description: The minimap mapped world z straight onto canvas y, but the camera sits south of its target looking north, so the far edge of the world is the top of the screen: the drawing, the view box and the entity dots were all mirrored against the map they sit beside. Filed after the fix, from the user's report.
close_reason: toPixels and the click mapping flip z against canvas y, and terrain patches draw upward from their sample so the flip leaves no seam.

title: Memoise the explored set instead of replaying the crawl
description: explored is recomputed from scratch over every turn and every entity whenever anything it reads changes, which is fine at 5,000 hexes and a handful of turns and will not be at 270,000 and hundreds. Cache it per turn and field version and extend it as turns are spent rather than replaying the whole crawl.
acceptance_criteria: Advancing a turn does not re-derive the whole crawl; rewinding still scrubs the fog exactly; the fog tests still pass.

title: Full-window page with no chrome
description: Map edge to edge, nothing on the page scrolling but the panel's own body, the panel and dial floating over the map. Under about 720px the panel starts collapsed and the dial scales down, so a phone gets map and controls rather than a wall of panel.
acceptance_criteria: No page-level scrollbar at any size; the map fills the window; a phone-width viewport is usable.

title: Minimap: the whole world, the entities and the view
description: A 2D canvas component, not Babylon. Samples the field every k-th hex into a cached image whenever the world changes, then each frame draws that image plus a dot per entity in its colour and a rectangle for the current view. Clicking maps the pixel back to a hex and moves the view there.
acceptance_criteria: The minimap shows the world, the entities and where the view is looking; clicking it lands there; it redraws without resampling the world on every frame.

title: World size control and its migration
description: worldRadius in the store with WORLD_SIZES small 60 / large 150 / huge 300, a picker in the panel beside the seed, and one appended migration adding map.world_radius plus the field on MapSnapshot, plain() and both ends of mapState. Changing the size starts the crawl over, as a new seed does: a different world is a different place and a shrunk one could strand an entity outside the rim.
acceptance_criteria: The picker changes the rim and the minimap; panning stops at the new edge; the size survives a reload.

title: Arrows take the colour of the entity whose path they are
description: Every path on the map is drawn in the same orange, so with several entities shown there is no telling whose line is whose. Arrows should carry the entity colour the panel and the token already use, which means one arrow mesh per colour rather than one for the lot.
acceptance_criteria: With all paths shown, each entity's arrows match its pawn and its row in the panel; a single path still draws as before.

title: Map and log refinements after the turn clock
description: A round of refinements asked for in session: brighter day and night lighting driven by the clock, a show-all-paths checkbox, the adventure log keeping every recorded turn (including ones wound back past) and jumping the crawl to a clicked turn, a clear-the-history button, an empty entity list being allowed, tokens leaping between hexes in an arc, and crowded hexes sharing their pawns side by side. Filed after the fact: the work was done straight from the prompts without a bead, which is the drift this project keeps catching.
close_reason: Delivered across the session: lighting, path checkboxes, adventure log with turn jumps, clear history, empty entity list, arc hop, crowded hexes, label wording.

title: Incremental fog diff once the board outgrows radius 40
description: Deferred from 9tn.7. The fog path is O(board): at radius 40 the whole-board clarity map plus setFog costs 0.31 ms per party step, and at radius 80 it is 2.4 ms. Both halves have to change together — diff the clarity map in HexCanvas so it carries only hexes whose clarity moved, and give HexGrid.setFog a sparse path so it stops scanning every instance. Measured numbers and reasoning are on 9tn.7; scripts/bench-fog.ts reruns them.
acceptance_criteria: A party step touches only the hexes whose clarity changed, in both the clarity map and the instance buffer; bench-fog.ts shows the fog cost no longer growing with board size.
notes: Reshaped by the windowed world (hexcrawl_web-mw8). The fog map is now built from the grid window rather than the whole board, so the cost is bounded by what is on screen (about 20k hexes at the widest zoom, far fewer at the usual one) instead of by the world, which at the huge size would be 271k. What remains is the same two halves: diff the clarity map so a step carries only the hexes that moved, and give setFog a sparse path so it stops scanning the whole window. Re-measure with scripts/bench-fog.ts before doing either.
close_reason: HexGrid.updateFog sparse path + HexCanvas steps the clarity map from visible/explored deltas (store exploredState); bench radius 40 to 80: stepped diff 0.009 to 0.019 ms, updateFog 0.008 to 0.072 ms, whole-window 0.229 to 1.950 ms. 451 tests, typecheck, lint pass

title: [epic] Session views and permissions: player vs DM
description: Eventually the crawl is watched through two windows: the players see their own parties and the ground they have uncovered, the DM sees everything and owns the entities only he controls. This epic covers what each view shows, who may queue actions for which entity, and how the two stay in step in one session. Nothing is built here yet: entities carry owner and hidden flags in hexcrawl_web-t3p, which is as far as ownership goes for now.
notes:
Rules (decided 2026-10-14): players order only owner=player entities; DM entities are DM-only even when visible. Clock (next turn, rewind, skip to dark/dawn) is DM-only. Players may rename/recolor entities they own; add/remove is DM-only. Players may edit inventories (1a1.3). Fog edits, terrain, roads, rivers, resources, notes, locations, events, encounter tables, map load/import/export/reseed, history clear: DM-only.
2026-10-15 user decision: the host is always the DM. DM/player switch is a debugging aid only: hidden unless the per-browser 'debug mode' checkbox (world panel, src/composables/useDebugMode.ts, localStorage hexcrawl.debug) is on; turning debug off forces dmView back to true. Player view for real comes from joining a session (05c.9).
2026-10-15 user decision (token flow): DM picks a token in the entity list and select-tool clicks place it (off map) or order it (on map); clicking the picked token in the list again unpicks it so clicks inspect hexes. Players may place their own token once (permissions 'place' = ownsTarget; store refuses a player re-placing a placed token). Joining adds a player token: 05c.11.
2026-10-15: role comes from the enter dialog (05c.12): Host and Work offline are DM, Join is player. DM/player switch stays debug-only.
2026-10-15: enter screen roles — Host = DM, Prepare = DM with fog off, Join = player.

title: A token per entity on the map
description: The scene draws one pawn today. Each entity needs its own token in its own colour, moving over the hexes its record says it entered, with hidden DM entities drawn only in the DM view.
acceptance_criteria: Several entities are visible and move independently as turns pass; hidden entities are absent unless the DM view is on.
close_reason: Token per entity via createTokenField; turn playback focuses the camera on each mover and walks its token hex by hex.

title: Turn-keyed persistence
description: Schema gains a turn table that the history hangs off, plus entity, action, entity_turn and queued_action tables; the journey table and the hour column go. Rewinding then acting deletes turn rows past the current turn and the cascades take the rest. Explored hexes are no longer saved: they are derived from the record.
acceptance_criteria: A crawl survives a reload with its turn, entities, record and queue intact; rewinding past recorded turns and acting leaves no orphan rows; migrations are appended, not edited.

title: Dial: turn arrows, skip to next phase, stars
description: DayNightDial gains a back arrow and a forward arrow that each spend one turn, plus a control that runs to the next dawn or dusk. The emblem sits at clock.index of TURNS_PER_PHASE - 1, and stars come out on night turns, which the original brief asked for and never got.
acceptance_criteria: Both arrows move the clock one turn and the emblem with it; the skip control lands on the next phase opening; stars show only at night; the rewind arrow is disabled at turn zero.

title: Let a watch pass without the party moving
description: Time only moved when the party did, so a party that wanted to wait out the dark, make camp or sit out a storm had no way to spend hours. A play control inside the dial winds the clock on by one watch — three hours — per press, matching the step the emblem takes on the arc so the two cannot disagree about how far a press moves the day. Four presses carry a phase from its opening to its turn. Nothing is logged and the party does not move: this is waiting, not travelling.
design: Advances by a watch rather than an hour so one press is one visible step of the emblem. HOURS_PER_WATCH and WATCHES_PER_PHASE live in src/time/clock.ts so the store and the dial read the same numbers instead of each carrying their own.
acceptance_criteria: A control in the dial advances the clock by one watch; the emblem steps with it and the phase turns over after the fourth press; the party's position and journey log are untouched; the advanced time persists; unit tested.
close_reason: Delivered: a control in the dial winds the clock on without moving the party. Superseded in shape by hexcrawl_web-t3p.4, which replaces the single watch button with turn arrows and a skip-to-phase control.

title: Decide and enforce what night does to travel
description: Decided: night shrinks sight and leaves pace alone. An entity's radius on a night turn is max(1, round(sight * 0.3)); travel is allowed after dark, but the party explores almost nothing and can walk straight past what it was looking for. The fog and vision code already take a radius, so no new mechanism is needed. Built as part of the store work in hexcrawl_web-t3p.3.
acceptance_criteria: Sight radius is cut on night turns and restored at dawn; the reduced radius is what the fog and sight overlay draw; unit tested.

title: Toggle: draw arrows for the whole logged path, or just the last leg
description: The route arrows only ever show the leg the party is walking or has just walked. Add a toggle that traces the whole journey log instead, so a crawl reads as one continuous trail. Off is the current behaviour. The trail is drawn up to the row the party is standing on and, while a route is still being walked, continues into the revealed stretch of it — so the arrows always form one unbroken line ending at the party rather than jumping across the map. The leg drawn after arrival is already in the log and is not drawn twice. Persisted like the other view toggles.
acceptance_criteria: A toggle switches the arrows between the whole logged path and the last leg; the drawn trail is contiguous in both modes, including after a recall part-way down the log; an animated leg in progress continues the trail rather than being hidden; the setting survives a reload; unit tested.
close_reason: Verified in the browser by the user.

title: Auto travel reveals only the endpoints, not the ground it crossed
description: Exploration accumulates from wherever the party stands, so an animated walk carves a corridor of revealed ground one step at a time. Auto travel never stands anywhere in between: it goes from one end of the leg to the other in a single move, so everything the party walked past stays under fog. The same leg walked at speed 1 and on auto leaves two different maps. Reveal along every hex of a committed leg, not just where it ended up.
acceptance_criteria: A leg walked on auto reveals the same ground as the same leg walked at a speed; the corridor is explored along its whole length; an animated walk is unaffected; unit tested against both speeds.
close_reason: Verified in the browser by the user.

title: Recall rolls the fog back to what was known at that step
description: Clicking a log row already moves the party back to that hex. The map does not follow: ground revealed by the steps being undone stays explored, so winding back leaves the party looking at terrain it has not seen yet from where it now stands. Make the explored set a function of how far down its log each party has actually walked — the union of what every traveler could see from each step up to the one it is standing on — and recompute it on recall. Uses the current sight radius rather than whatever was set at the time, which is the party's eyes as they are now.
acceptance_criteria: Recalling to a step un-explores ground first seen after it; ground seen at or before that step stays explored; walking forward again re-reveals it; every traveler contributes what it has seen up to its own position; unit tested.
close_reason: Verified in the browser by the user.

title: Clear the journey log, and reset it when the party turns off the record
description: Replaces the double-click rewind (hexcrawl_web-9tn.15), which deleted history. The log now keeps everything by default. A 'clear the log' button starts the record again from where the party stands, seeding it with the current position as step zero. Walking on from a hex the party was recalled to either retraces what the log already says, which changes nothing and just advances the party along it, or contradicts it: a leg that leaves the recorded path means the recorded future never happened, so the log is cleared and restarted from the hex the party turned off at, with the new direction as its first steps. Which log entry the party is standing on is tracked as an index, because a crawl can cross the same hex twice.
acceptance_criteria: A clear button empties the log and seeds it with the party's current position at zero km; recalling to a step and re-walking the recorded path leaves the log untouched and moves the party along it; walking past the end of the recorded path appends only the new ground; a leg that diverges clears the log and restarts it from the turn-off hex; the row the party stands on is marked exactly, even when the same hex appears twice; unit tested.
close_reason: Verified in the browser by the user.

title: Rewind the journey by double-clicking a log entry
description: Single-clicking a journey row stands the party back on that hex and leaves the record alone. Double-clicking it winds the journey back for real: the party stands there again and every step it took afterwards is struck from the log. Keyed on the step index rather than the hex, because a crawl can cross the same hex twice and only the row that was clicked should decide where the cut falls. Explored ground is left alone — rewinding where the party is does not un-see the terrain; 'forget the map' is the tool for that.
acceptance_criteria: Double-clicking a journey row moves the party to that step and drops every later step; the clicked step survives; a pending destination is cleared and the drawn path reset; an out-of-range step is refused; explored hexes are untouched; single click stays non-destructive; unit tested.
close_reason: Reverted at the user's request: deleting history was the wrong trade. Superseded by hexcrawl_web-9tn.16, which keeps the log and clears it only on an explicit button or a divergent leg.

title: One click per leg: selection commits the walked route
description: The party needed a 'move party here' button to take up its destination, which made every leg two gestures and let the token fall behind the route. Selection now carries it: the first click puts the party on the map, and each click after that plans the next leg and commits the one before it. Clicking the hex the party stands on calls off the planned leg. A route still mid-animation is being replanned rather than finished, so it commits nothing. The button is gone.
acceptance_criteria: No 'move party here' button; the first click places the party; a later click commits the previous leg and sets the next goal; clicking the party's own hex clears the goal without taking the party off the map; a click during an unfinished animation replans without committing; unit tested.
close_reason: Journey log, one-click legs and log recall landed; auto-arrival regression fixed and verified by the suite.

title: Journey log: record every hex the party walks
description: The map keeps where the party is but not how it got there. Record an ordered log of every hex the party actually travels through, with the cost and terrain of each step, so the session has a readable history of its pathing. The log persists in the SQLite save alongside the rest of the map state, which also pins the party's last position to something the reload can read back rather than infer. Shown in the side panel as a running list. Single party for now; per-traveler logs come with hexcrawl_web-9tn.4.
design: Entries are appended when a journey is committed rather than while the reveal animation runs, so an abandoned half-walked route leaves no false history, and auto mode logs the same hexes as animated mode.
acceptance_criteria: Committing a move appends one entry per hex of the route, in order, with per-step km and terrain; the log survives a reload; total distance travelled is derivable from it; the panel lists the journey; unit and round-trip tested.
close_reason: Journey log, one-click legs and log recall landed; auto-arrival regression fixed and verified by the suite.

title: Reveal animation and fog across chained legs
description: The reveal animation walks a whole waypoint chain rather than one leg, and fog/exploration accumulate along it. With several travelers, exploration is the union of what each has seen.
acceptance_criteria: Play walks every leg of a chain in order without resetting between legs; explored hexes accumulate across the chain; multiple travelers each contribute to the explored set; unit tested.
close_reason: Superseded by the turn clock. The reveal animation it describes is gone: movement happens because turns pass, hexcrawl_web-t3p.7 plays each turn back, and exploration is derived from the record as the union of what every entity has seen. Closed over its dependency on 9tn.4.2, which no longer gates it.

title: Traveler list UI and multiple party tokens
description: A selectable list panel of travelers and groups, and one token per traveler rendered on the map instead of the single pawn. Selecting a row in the list, or clicking a token, sets what map clicks route. Grouped travelers read as a group in the list.
acceptance_criteria: List shows travelers and groups and drives selection; each traveler renders its own token at its own hex; the selected traveler or group is visually distinct; token instancing is unit tested.
close_reason: Delivered by hexcrawl_web-t3p.3 and t3p.6: the panel lists entities and selects one, and every entity has its own token in its own colour, with crowded hexes sharing side by side.

title: Caravans carry riders: parties join and leave by position
description: Caravans are the only grouping. A caravan-kind entity houses other entities (riders). A non-caravan entity with no route left that stands on a caravan's hex at the end of a turn joins it. A rider moves with the caravan at the caravan's pace. Giving a rider a move order takes it out of the caravan; it walks at its own pace from the caravan's hex, and leaving costs nothing extra. Membership is part of each entity's per-turn state, so rewinds are exact and no group tables are needed.
acceptance_criteria: Party on a caravan's hex joins it; rider follows the caravan route at the caravan's pace; ordering a rider away makes it leave with no extra cost; membership is unit tested and survives reload.

title: Multi-leg routes: waypoint chain with per-leg and total km
description: A move order is one route from where an entity stands. Chaining means an order can carry waypoints: the entity walks leg after leg as the turns pass, the panel reports turns and km per leg and for the chain, and a new order still calls the whole chain off. Reshaped by the turn queue in hexcrawl_web-t3p: this now lands on Action and the pending route in src/entities, not on a start/goal pair.
acceptance_criteria: Waypoints append and remove; the route chains legs in order through findRoute; per-leg km and total km are exposed by the store and shown in the UI; unit tested including empty, single and many-leg chains.
notes: Implemented: waypoints on move Action + EntityState (popped in resolve walk), chainRoute/joinLegs in terrain/travel, store legs/routeTurns/removeWaypoint, shift-click appends via scene onSelect(hex, append), panel legs list, schema migration 8 adds waypoints columns. typecheck/lint/372 tests green. Pending: browser check before close.

title: Traveler model and store: list, add, remove, select
description: Introduce a Traveler entity (id, name, colour, position hex) and hold an ordered list of them in the hexMap store, replacing the single implicit party. Travelers can be added, removed and renamed, and exactly one traveler or group is the current selection that map clicks act on. The existing single-party behaviour becomes one traveler in the list so nothing regresses.
acceptance_criteria: Store exposes travelers, selection, add/remove/rename/select actions; the current party token is one traveler in the list; existing party/route behaviour is unchanged for a single traveler; unit tested.
close_reason: Verified in the browser by the user.

title: Relief slider changed nothing: matrix instance buffer was static
description: The grid created its thin-instance matrix buffer with staticBuffer=true, from when tile heights were written once at build time. Live terrain controls rewrite those matrices, but a static buffer cannot be re-uploaded, so thinInstanceBufferUpdated('matrix') never reached the GPU. Colours used a non-static buffer and did update, which is why sea level looked half-alive while relief looked dead. Verified with a probe: staticBuffer=true leaves world0 and matrixBuffer isUpdatable()=false.
acceptance_criteria: Both instance buffers are updatable and a regression test asserts it.
close_reason: Matrix buffer created non-static; regression test asserts world0 and instanceColor stay updatable

title: Reserve the sight bonus for mountains and peaks
description: Every step up currently widens the sight radius, so walking from a beach into grass or forest already buys extra reach. Only real high ground should: keep the bonus for the top two bands and rename rock and snow to mountains and peaks while the terrain vocabulary is being settled.
acceptance_criteria: Water, sand, grass and forest all see the same distance; mountains and peaks each add reach; the terrain ids read mountains and peaks throughout.
close_reason: vantageFloor gates the sight bonus above the treeline; rock and snow renamed to mountains and peaks

title: Only ground above the party blocks its view
description: Line of sight is pure slope maths, so a ridge below the party still casts a shadow into the ground past it. Standing on a height should mean seeing over everything lower: only a hex on a step above the party can get in the way, and the slope test then decides how far its shadow reaches.
acceptance_criteria: A hex at or below the party's level never blocks; a hex above it blocks by the existing slope test; looking down from a summit clears the whole disc; existing ridge and peak behaviour from lower ground is unchanged.
close_reason: Only hexes on a step above the party contribute a blocking claim; the slope test then decides how far that shadow reaches

title: Split elevation into mechanical levels and rendered height
description: Line of sight, blocking and climb cost all read the continuous rendered height, so mechanics turn on differences too small to see and the climb threshold never fires. Give every tile an integer level for mechanics and keep the smooth height for rendering, then spread the rendered range further apart for more contrast in the terrain.
acceptance_criteria: TerrainTile carries an integer level alongside its rendered elevation; LOS and climb cost read the level; rendering reads the height; the rendered range is visibly taller and level order matches height order.
close_reason: TerrainTile carries a band-pinned integer level; LOS and climb cost read it, rendering keeps the smooth height. Climb share on generated terrain went from inert to 12.3% of adjacent steps.

title: Pinia store survives HMR and crashes reloaded components
description: hexMap.ts never called acceptHMRUpdate, so the live store instance outlived every hot update. A component hot-reloading against a store that had since grown a field crashed on it — hit while adding blocked to the sight field, where HexCanvas threw 'store.blocked is not iterable' against a stale store.
acceptance_criteria: Editing the store hot-updates its instance instead of leaving a stale one behind.

title: Sight field overlay showing what the terrain blocks
description: Fog shows where the party has been but not why it cannot see further. A toggle draws the sight disc as translucent plates over the terrain: cool glaze on hexes in line of sight, red shade on hexes within reach that something is standing in front of, so a ridge reads as the shadow it casts.
acceptance_criteria: Panel toggle turns the overlay on and off; plates are translucent and sit over the terrain they describe; blocked hexes inside the sight radius are visually distinct from visible ones; vision reports blocked hexes and the whole path is unit tested.
close_reason: Sight overlay shipped: fieldOfView reports blocked hexes, visionOverlay draws translucent lit/shadow plates, panel toggle

title: Persist map state to a local SQLite DB
description: src/persistence/ is empty. Stand up a browser-local SQLite database (sqlite-wasm, OPFS sahpool VFS) as the save layer, and cover the state that already exists: terrain controls (seed, scale, seaLevel, relief), route endpoints, explored-hex set, sight radius, fog/showSight/allowWater flags. Terrain tiles are NOT stored — they are derived from seed + controls. First pass only; the schema is expected to be refined once travelers and groups land (see hexcrawl_web-9tn.4).
design: sqlite-wasm over localStorage because the sandbox is heading for a shared live session and a real relational schema now maps onto a server DB later. OPFS sahpool VFS avoids needing COOP/COEP headers. Tests open :memory: so they exercise the same SQL.
acceptance_criteria: A versioned SQLite schema opens in the browser and persists across reload; save/load round-trips every store field listed above; loading restores terrain, route endpoints and explored hexes; schema version is recorded and checked; round-trip is integration tested against a real in-memory SQLite.
close_reason: Verified in the browser: OPFS-backed SQLite restores terrain, endpoints and explored hexes across a reload.

title: Travelers: selectable parties, convoy groups, multi-leg routes
description: Today the map has one implicit party and a single start/goal pair. Replace that with a list of traveler objects. Travelers can be selected from a list; several can be joined into a group (caravan/convoy) that shares one path, or split off to walk routes of their own. Each traveler's route is a chain of waypoints with per-leg and total distance. Selecting a group routes the whole group; selecting a single traveler reroutes just that one. Broken into children.
acceptance_criteria: Parent is done when all children are closed.
notes: Half of this epic landed as hexcrawl_web-t3p instead: entities, selection, a token each, and the schema. What is left here is waypoint chains (9tn.4.2) and convoy groups (9tn.4.3), both reshaped onto the turn queue.

title: Live terrain controls: seed, scale, sea level, relief
description: Terrain options are currently code-only defaults. Expose seed, scale, sea level and relief in the side panel so maps can be tuned in the browser and regenerated without an edit-reload cycle.
acceptance_criteria: Panel exposes seed/scale/seaLevel/relief; changing a value regenerates terrain and refreshes the scene; route and party state react sensibly to regeneration.
close_reason: Panel exposes seed/scale/seaLevel/relief; grid re-terrains in place via HexGrid.setTiles so the camera, party and fog survive a regenerate

title: Climb threshold makes elevation inert on generated terrain
description: stepCostKm now doubles only when the next hex is at least 2 units higher, which correctly stops a party being charged double to wade ashore. But neighbouring hexes on the generated map differ by 0.39 units at the median and 2.05 at the absolute maximum, so only 2 of 29040 adjacent steps qualify. Every route now costs exactly the flat distance and terrain no longer deflects travel at all. Either the threshold drops to around 0.75-1, or terrain relief rises so neighbouring hexes differ more sharply.
acceptance_criteria: A meaningful share of uphill steps cost double, and routes measurably prefer contouring over climbing on the default map
close_reason: TerrainTile carries a band-pinned integer level; LOS and climb cost read it, rendering keeps the smooth height. Climb share on generated terrain went from inert to 12.3% of adjacent steps.

title: Direction arrows along the route
description: Colouring hexes showed the route but not which way it ran. Thin-instanced 3D arrows sit on the seam between consecutive hexes, pointing in the direction of travel, with rounded top edges and a slow hover cycle.
acceptance_criteria: One arrow per step centred on the gap, yawed to travel direction, clearing the taller hex, not pickable, bobbing in a loop
close_reason: Shipped and verified in browser; covered by tests

title: Animated route reveal
description: A traced route appeared instantly, with no sense of travel. A speed slider (auto, 1x, 2x, 3x) plus a start button walks the route hex by hex, counting hexes and kilometres as it goes.
acceptance_criteria: Slider and start button in the panel; reveal paced by requestAnimationFrame; rewinds on route or speed change; auto behaves as before
close_reason: Shipped and verified in browser; covered by tests

title: More pronounced terrain relief
description: Peaks read too flat against the hex size. Terrain relief raised 30 percent, leaving sea level and shoreline heights untouched.
acceptance_criteria: Peak elevation 4.47 to 5.67 units; water and shore unchanged
close_reason: Shipped and verified in browser; covered by tests

title: Zoom-linked camera tilt
description: The isometric tilt was fixed at 54.7 degrees. Tilt now tracks zoom so the view drops toward the horizon up close and flattens to a map view pulled back.
acceptance_criteria: Tilt swings between 15 and 49 degrees above the horizon across the zoom 10-20 band, log interpolated, pinned outside it

title: Measure and trim the cost of a fog recompute
description: Every party step walks a hex line per target hex, roughly O(radius^3), and then rebuilds a fog map covering the whole board. Fine at a 40-hex radius and three steps per second, but both scale badly. Measure before optimising; shadowcasting would replace the per-target line walk if it turns out to matter.
design:
Measured with scripts/bench-fog.ts (bun run bench): NullEngine grid, real
terrain, warmed loop. Times are per party step, ms.

Board radius 40 (4921 hexes, what MapView ships):
  sightFrom r=5 (default)      0.052
  sightFrom r=10               0.268
  sightFrom r=14 (max)         0.699
  whole-board fog map          0.234
  incremental fog diff         0.007
  explored set copy            0.010
  setFog (one step moved)      0.074
  setFog (nothing changed)     0.070
  -> one step: 0.37 ms at r=5, 1.02 ms at r=14

Board radius 80 (19441 hexes), same sight radii:
  sightFrom r=14               0.664   (unchanged)
  whole-board fog map          1.729
  incremental fog diff         0.016
  setFog (one step moved)      0.702
  -> one step: 2.5 ms at r=5, 3.1 ms at r=14

DECISION: no shadowcasting, no incremental fog diff. Neither pays for itself
yet.

Shadowcasting is the wrong target. sightFrom is O(r^3), but r is hard-capped by
maxRadius 14, so it does not scale with the board at all: 0.66 ms at radius 80
is the same 0.70 ms as at radius 40. Worst case is 0.7 ms once every third of a
second. Shadowcasting would buy back at most that, and 0.05 ms at the default
sight of 5.

The fog path is what actually scales, and it is already the larger half. At
ship size the fog map plus setFog is 0.31 ms against 0.05 ms of sight; four
times the board takes it to 2.4 ms. An incremental diff is 30x cheaper than the
whole-board rebuild and is bounded by the sight disc rather than the board.
But it only half-pays: HexGrid.setFog still scans all 4921 instances to find
the few dozen that moved, and that is roughly half the fog cost. Doing the diff
without also giving setFog a changed-hexes path leaves most of the win on the
table.

Revisit when the board goes past radius ~60 (~11k hexes) or steps run faster
than 3/sec. The change then is the fog pair together — diff the clarity map in
HexCanvas and take a sparse update in setFog — not the line-of-sight walk.
acceptance_criteria: Cost of one visible/fog recompute is measured at full map size and a high sight radius; a decision is recorded on whether shadowcasting or an incremental fog diff is worth it.
close_reason: Measured; decision recorded in design. Neither shadowcasting nor an incremental fog diff is worth it at ship size. Follow-up filed for the fog diff.

title: Flatten unexplored hexes so fog does not leak elevation
description: Fogged tiles keep their real prism height, so mountains still poke out of ground nobody has seen and their silhouette gives away terrain the fog is meant to hide. Flattening unexplored tiles means rewriting their instance matrices, which the grid currently uploads once at build time.
acceptance_criteria: Unexplored hexes render at a flat height; explored and visible hexes keep their terrain height; the matrix buffer updates without rebuilding the grid.
notes:
Perf pass after user reported bad performance and too-dense clouds: 4 puffs per hex with per-pixel 4-octave fbm in the shader overdrew ~10-20 blended layers across the bank. Now 1 puff per hex (1.9-2.4x hex size, opacity 0.72) sampling a 128px RGBA atlas of 4 puff shapes drawn once on the CPU (red = light, alpha = thickness); shape index rides in the unused matrix slot m[3]. Colour uploads cover only the dirty index range. Not yet measured in the browser: check with the } RenderStats overlay.
Density/variety pass (user: too thin, wants noise-driven shape variety): atlas is now 3x3 = 9 shapes, each 3-5 overlapping lobes eroded by fbm noise with a flat belly. A slow fbm thickness field over the world (clumps ~9 hexes wide) drives each puff's width (2-3.6x hex size), height/aspect, opacity (0.62 thin to 1 thick) and rise above the ceiling, so the bank forms clumps and breaks. Per-puff random stretch and a small turn (matrix slot m[7]); shape index in m[3]; opacity in the instance colour alpha. Still one quad per hex.
Scale/colour pass (user: looking better, scale up 50%, mostly white): puff width now 3-5.4x hex size; atlas shading narrowed to 0.90-1.0; base cloud colour 0.98/0.985/1; scene shade = warmth * min(1, 0.45 + sun*0.25 + sky*0.3), about 1 by day and ~0.8 moonlit at night.
Daylight pass (user: thick clouds bigger than thin, keep the blueish night and grade into it across turns, day too bright every other turn): puff width 1.8x hex size thin to 6x thick with +-8% jitter. Day brightness flicker came from daylightFor: turns 1-2 had sun height 0.87 (sun 1.19, sky 0.97, steep light) vs 0 on turns 0/3 (sun 0.8, sky 0.75, grazing light at a quarter of the top-face brightness). Now the light sweeps sideways only at a fixed elevation with constant day sun/sky. All light values blend day->night by a cosine coolness over the 8-turn day centred on midnight (0.31, 0.04, 0.04, 0.31, 0.69, 0.96, 0.96, 0.69); moon colour cooler blue (0.62, 0.72, 1).

User did not like the implementation; all cloud code reverted, fog darkening of unseen hexes kept as it was. The daylight fix found along the way lives on in hexcrawl_web-9tn.22.

title: Decide how boats and water travel work
description: Water is currently all-or-nothing: impassable, or the same 10km per hex as land. A hexcrawl probably wants boats, coastal versus open sea, or a distinct water speed. Needs a rules decision before the travel model hardens.
acceptance_criteria: Water travel rules decided and reflected in stepCostKm
notes: Decision 2026-10-12: option B. Ships are an entity kind that carries riders like caravans. Ships move only on water and coast hexes (land next to water), ~3 hexes/turn, better sight at sea. Land kinds cannot enter water. Boarding = 9tn.4.3 riding rule (party ends turn on ship hex); embarking therefore only at coast. Riders cannot be ordered off while at sea. Global allow_water toggle replaced by per-kind movement. Coastal vs open sea (option C) deferred.

title: Measure hover picking cost at full map size
description: Hover runs scene.pick on every pointer move against roughly 5000 thin instances. It has never been profiled. If it costs more than a millisecond or two per move, replace it with a ray-plane intersection against y=0 plus worldToHex, which is O(1) and uses the already-tested hex library.
acceptance_criteria: Pointer-move pick cost measured at radius 40; either confirmed acceptable or replaced with the ground-plane approach
notes:
Windowing changed the shape of this: scene.pick now runs against the grid window (about 20k instances at the default max zoom of 60, and far fewer at the usual zoom) rather than against the whole world, which at the huge world size would have been 271k. Still unmeasured in a browser; the ground-plane alternative is unchanged as a fallback.
Measured with scripts/bench-pick.ts (bun bench:pick), NullEngine on Bun at 1920x1080, huge world (r300), 400 pointers. NOT a browser - absolute numbers are CPU-only, the ratio is the signal. scene.pick: ~1.7-1.9ms/move at zoom 40 (7680 instances), ~17-24ms/move at max zoom 200 (72576 instances). Bare y=0 ray + worldToHex: ~0.001ms but lands up to ~2 hexes behind tall hexes at the 41deg lean (elevations reach ~7.7). Replaced hover/tap pick with hexUnderPointer (src/engine/scene.ts) -> hexUnderRay (src/engine/groundPick.ts): walks the ray from the grid bounds' top down to y=0 at 16 samples per hex size, takes the first sample below the drawn height (grid.heightAt, so fog-flattened hexes count) and inside the inset tile (grid.tileSize, so the border gap misses like scene.pick did). ~0.009-0.012ms/move. Agrees with scene.pick on 386-394/400 pointers; the rest are rim cases (bevel/corner clips) off by one neighbour. picking.test.ts now runs every screen-picking case against both pickers, plus a tall-hex case.

title: Trim the Babylon bundle
description: The production bundle is 1.09 MB, 270 kB gzipped, most of it Babylon's StandardMaterial shader set. Worth checking whether a lighter material or a narrower set of side-effect imports cuts it materially before the app grows.
acceptance_criteria: Bundle size measured per dependency and either reduced or documented as acceptable
notes: Measured 2026-09-13 with vite build --sourcemap + source-map-explorer on main chunk. Before: 1138 kB / 294 kB gzip. Babylon Meshes 296 kB, Materials 205, Engines 124, Cameras 92, scene 81, app 53, vue runtime-core 36, vue-router 22. MeshBuilder barrel pulled every builder (~90 kB: decal, polyhedron, tiledPlane, goldberg, text...). Fix: import CreateGround/CreateCylinder/CreateSphere/CreatePlane from Meshes/Builders/* in scene.ts, partyToken.ts, waypointMarkers.ts. After: 1025 kB / 262 kB gzip (-113 kB, -32 kB gzip). Remaining is accepted: StandardMaterial + material helpers (~185 kB) only go with a custom ShaderMaterial and hand-written lighting; ArcRotateCamera drags inputs, DeviceInput and camera behaviors (framing/autoRotation/bouncing) - filed as follow-up. Lazy chunks (texture loaders, WGSL shaders) never load on WebGL and do not count.
close_reason: Main chunk 1138->1025 kB (294->262 gzip) by dropping MeshBuilder barrel; remainder measured and documented

title: Swap ArcRotateCamera for a lighter camera
